providers.name: @TippyFlits (ezpdpz-calib)
providers.note: A PDP storage provider running Curio, in the UK. Registry id 9 on Calibration; it also runs the PieceWork provider kit, which is what lets it sell compute. Has every job image built, and runs the GPU ones on an NVIDIA T4, one at a time. The CPU-only video-index and photo-restore are deliberately not listed here: with a card on the machine there is no reason to offer the slow one.

pii-redact:v1.name: Find and remove personal data in my documents
pii-redact:v1.note: Writes a redacted copy of each document plus a report of what it found and where.

embed:v1.name: Make my documents searchable by meaning (embeddings)
embed:v1.note: Turns documents into vectors so they can be searched by meaning rather than by keyword. Transcripts count as documents — this is what makes a recording searchable.

embed-gpu:v1.name: Make my documents searchable by meaning (embeddings) (on the card)
embed-gpu:v1.note: The same embeddings on a provider's GPU. Not measured against the processor here, so order it for throughput on a large archive rather than on a promised speed-up.

indexer:v1.name: Build a search index of my files
indexer:v1.note: A plain keyword index. The simplest job here, useful for checking the plumbing works.

query:v1.name: Run my SQL over my tables
query:v1.note: Put a .sql file in the data set alongside your tables; it runs over the csv, parquet and json already stored here and returns the rows, so gigabytes stay put and only the answer moves.

image-clean:v1.name: Take the people, or the background, out of my photographs
outputs: (a -clean.png and -mask.png per file, plus a report)
image-clean:v1.note: Put a line in what.txt saying background or people. It writes the cleaned image and the mask beside it, so you can see what the model decided to remove rather than taking its word for it. A photo archive is the case where moving the compute to the data pays best, because the inputs are large and the answer is another image. Not yet exercised on a real photograph.

image-clean-gpu:v1.name: Take the people, or the background, out of my photographs (on the card)
outputs: (a -clean.png and -mask.png per file, plus a report)
image-clean-gpu:v1.note: The same job and the same models on a provider's GPU. Segmentation is work a card does well, but by how much is unmeasured here, so treat these two rows as the same result at different speeds until there are numbers.

video-index:v1.name: Index what is in my video
video-index:v1.note: Watches the video once and writes down what is in it and when — a person at 00:04:12, a car at 00:07:30, a shot change just before. The index is small enough to read and search, which is the point: on one test the video was 24.5 MB and the index was 154 bytes, so the answer came back 159,193 times smaller than the question. That is the case where sending your video somewhere to be processed makes least sense. On a processor it runs at about 2.7 times real time, so an hour of footage is roughly 22 minutes of work.

video-index-gpu:v1.name: Index what is in my video (on the card)
video-index-gpu:v1.note: The same index on a provider's GPU, and now with a number. Measured on a storage provider's own T4 over ten minutes of footage: 27.4 frames a second, 21.9 s for the 600 frames examined, 32 s end to end including container start and model load — against 2.7 frames a second on a processor, so ten times faster, and an hour of footage drops from about 22 minutes of work to 2.2. It read 48.7 MB of video and wrote a 15 KB index. The provider's own caveat, worth keeping: that film is 320x240, so higher-resolution footage will be slower per frame. Decoding also stays on the processor here, so a faster card would start to wait on it.

video-gen:v1.name: Build a video from my pictures, and record what it came from
video-gen:v1.note: Builds a video from the pictures you pick, and writes beside it a record of exactly what it was made from: every input by its sha256, the prompt you gave, and the version it was built on. Order it again and it builds the next version on top of the last, all in the same data set — so you end up with a chain of versions where each one names its parent, and anyone holding the pieces can check that claim without trusting the provider. Put your prompt in a file called prompt.json: {"prompt": "...", "seconds": 4, "fps": 12}. The generator is deliberately simple for now; the interesting part is the record, not the picture.

photo-restore:v1.name: Enlarge and clean up my photographs
photo-restore:v1.note: Four times the width and height, with detail reconstructed rather than interpolated (Real-ESRGAN). On a processor this took 17.6 seconds for a 320x320 image, which scales to roughly 35 minutes for a normal 12-megapixel photograph — so order the card version for anything bigger than a thumbnail, or for more than a handful.

photo-restore-gpu:v1.name: Enlarge and clean up my photographs (on the card)
photo-restore-gpu:v1.note: The same restoration on a provider’s GPU. Measured on a storage provider’s own T4: 1.2 seconds to take a 320x320 image to 1280x1280, and 2.7 seconds for the job end to end, against 17.6 seconds for the same image on a processor. About fifteen times, which over an archive is the difference between weeks and months.

transcode:v1.name: Re-encode my video, smaller
transcode:v1.note: Re-encodes each video to 480p and writes a thumbnail beside it. The original is untouched unless you choose a policy that replaces it.

transcode-gpu:v1.name: Re-encode my video, smaller (on the card)
transcode-gpu:v1.note: The same transcode through the card's dedicated encoder (NVENC), which every card bought for sealing has. Of all the GPU rows here this is where the largest difference is most likely, but NVENC buys throughput rather than fidelity: at the same file size the picture is usually a little worse. Unmeasured here.

transcribe:v1.name: Transcribe my recordings, searchable by the moment
outputs: (a transcript, subtitles and segments per recording)
transcribe:v1.note: Writes three files back per recording: a transcript with the time at the start of every paragraph (read it, or order embeddings over it and search by meaning), subtitles any video player will load, and a short report saying how long the audio was and how fast it ran. On a processor this is roughly real time, so an hour of audio is an hour of compute.

transcribe-gpu:v1.name: Transcribe my recordings, searchable by the moment (on the card)
outputs: (a transcript, subtitles and segments per recording)
transcribe-gpu:v1.note: Measured on a storage provider's own hardware over the same 94.7 minutes of audio: 9x real time on two EPYC 7282 processors, 22x on an RTX A4000, and 15x for the larger large-v3-turbo model on that card. So the card is worth about 2.4x on the same model, and the better model gives some of that back for accuracy on names, which is what matters in an archive you intend to search. About 360 hours of audio a day on a card that would otherwise be idle. Needs about 6 GB of VRAM: an A4000, 3090, 4090 or V100 all clear it, and no H100 is required.

term-count-proved:v1.name: Count a term, and prove it ran on my data
term-count-proved:v1.note: The provider is paid only if a zero-knowledge proof convinces the chain that the count was computed over exactly the pieces you named. Delivering the right answer is not enough — it has to be the right answer about your data. Proving takes about ten minutes, so this job's deadline is an hour rather than the usual twenty minutes. Costs four times as much to prove as the attested version of the same job, which is why it costs four times as much to order.

term-count-attested:v1.name: Count a term, and prove the count — without proving whose data it was
term-count-attested:v1.note: The chain verifies the proof, so the count itself is not in doubt. What it does not check is which bytes were counted: the proof commits to a sha256 of each input rather than to its Filecoin piece CID, and nothing on chain ties those digests to the pieces you pay to store. They are recorded in the delivering transaction and written into the result, so you can retrieve a piece, hash it, and see whether it matches — evidence after the fact rather than a condition on payment. A quarter the price because it is a quarter the proving cost: 24 cycles a byte against 99. Order the bound job if you want the chain to enforce that the count was taken over your data.

ocr:v1.name: Read my scanned pages into text
ocr:v1.note: Tesseract on the provider's processor, or a neural detector on its card where it has one. A scanned archive is large and its text is tiny, so moving the images to the compute costs far more than moving the compute to the images.

ocr-gpu:v1.name: Read my scanned pages into text (on the card)
ocr-gpu:v1.note: A neural detector on the provider's card instead of tesseract on its processor. This is the one row where a GPU may buy accuracy as well as speed, because the classical engine degrades on skew, noise and low DPI where a neural one holds up. Both numbers are still missing — pages a minute and error rate on the same pages — and faster but no more accurate would be the weaker result.

extract:v1.name: Pull the facts out of my documents
extract:v1.note: Finds the counterparty, date, amount, currency and payment terms in each document and returns them as JSON. A 1.5-billion-parameter model runs entirely on the provider's hardware with no network, which is the point: the documents that most need this are the ones that cannot be sent to someone else's API.

extract-gpu:v1.name: Pull the facts out of my documents (on the card)
extract-gpu:v1.note: The same extraction with the model's layers on the card. Token generation is bound by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic, roughly 400 GB/s on an A4000 against perhaps 50 on a server processor, so expect several times faster and not the twenty people assume on hearing GPU. This image has not been built successfully yet, so no provider can currently take it.

frame-similarity:v1.name: Find where my video changes
outputs: (a -similarity.txt and a -cuts.json per video, plus a report)
frame-similarity:v1.note: Compares each sampled frame with the one before it and says where the picture changed enough to be a new shot. The answer is a list of cut points, which is what lets a video be stored as segments instead of one file — and that is what lets the next version of it point at the segments it did not change rather than storing them again. Two videos sharing half their frames share 0.0% of their bytes once encoded, so the sharing has to be built in at the cut points rather than discovered afterwards. No model and no GPU: this is histogram arithmetic, many times real time on a processor, which is why it is the cheapest row here.

image-index:v1.name: Index what is in my images
outputs: (an -index.txt per image, one image-index.json, plus a report)
image-index:v1.note: Looks at every image once and writes down what is in it and where — a person, a car, a boat, with a box and a confidence for each. The same thing the video indexer does, for the archives that are folders of stills rather than footage: robotics training data, satellite and scientific imagery, web crawls. The index is small enough to read and search, which is the point: the archive stays where it is and only the answer travels. Faces are detected and never identified — no face embeddings, no matching between images, no database of people, so it cannot tell you who someone is or that two photographs show the same person. GDPR Article 9 treats biometric data as special category when it is processed to uniquely identify someone; detection without identification does not meet that test, and the job's own report says so. Order it with FACES=0 to turn even the detection off.

image-index-gpu:v1.name: Index what is in my images (on the card)
outputs: (an -index.txt per image, one image-index.json, plus a report)
image-index-gpu:v1.note: The same index, and the same limits on faces, with the detector on a provider's GPU. This is the cleaner GPU measurement of the two indexers: the video one is held back by decoding frames on the processor, and a folder of JPEGs has no such ceiling, so what the card is worth shows up undiluted. Nobody has run it on a card yet, so there is no number here — the processor does about 3 images a second on this machine, and that is the figure to beat.

frame-stability:v1.name: Prove whether something moved
outputs: (a -stability.txt and a -stability.json per video, plus a report)
frame-stability:v1.note: Reads every frame, not a sample, and tracks one region named in track.json beside the video. The useful answer is usually a negative: it did not move, in any frame, and here are the per-frame coordinates. The point of publishing the coordinates is that nobody has to take the verdict on trust — the video is stored, the method is fixed, and the same job over the same piece gives the same table, so anyone holding the pieces can check it. No model and no card: normalised cross-correlation in a small window.

image-caption-gpu:v1.name: Describe my images in words (on the card)
outputs: (a -caption.txt per image, one image-caption.json, plus a report)
image-caption-gpu:v1.note: Describes each picture in a sentence instead of picking from a fixed list. This answers the one real limit of “Index what is in my images”: that job's detector knows exactly eighty COCO categories, and racing car, helmet and wheel are not among them — so photographs of Formula 1 cars came back as a truck and an airplane. Not a bug and not tunable; the model has no word for what it is looking at. A vision-language model has no fixed vocabulary. Florence-2-base, about 0.5 GB in fp16, which no sealing card will notice. GPU only on purpose and it refuses without a card: seconds an image on a processor against well under one on a T4, and a run that quietly used the processor would report a number nobody could compare with the detector row. Not yet run by anyone, on any card.

video-gen-gpu:v1.name: Build a video from my pictures, with a model (on the card)
video-gen-gpu:v1.note: The same loop and the same record, with Stable Video Diffusion instead of the deliberately simple motion generator. Identical output contract — version-N.mp4 beside a version-N.json naming every input by its sha256, the prompt, and the version it was built on — so the chain of takes, the client page and the storage cannot tell which generator ran. The model invents the motion from your last picture rather than panning across a still. GPU only and it refuses without a card: a diffusion video model on a processor is hours per clip, which is not a slower service but no service. The image is large, about 12 GB, because the weights are baked in — jobs run with no network. Not yet run by anyone, on any card.

video-search-gpu:v1.name: Make my video searchable by description (on the card)
outputs: (a -vectors.npy and a -search.txt per video, plus a report)
video-search-gpu:v1.note: Embeds each sampled frame into the same space as text, so the question can be any phrase — “a red single-seater on a wet track”, “an empty grandstand” — and the answer is the moments that match, with timestamps. Put the phrases in queries.json. This generalises “Index what is in my video”, which runs a detector that knows eighty fixed categories and can never be asked about anything else. The frame vectors are written beside the video on purpose: describing the archive is the expensive pass and every question after it is a dot product, which is the economic case for doing this where the data already sits. CLIP ViT-B/32, about 600 MB. GPU only, and it refuses without a card. Not yet run by anyone.

embed-live:v1.name: Keep my data set searchable
embed-live:v1.note: Whenever you add a document, it is turned into vectors next to your files and written back into the same data set. You never order anything — what you are buying is that your data set stays searchable as it changes.

redact-live:v1.name: Keep my data set clean
redact-live:v1.note: Every document you add is scanned for personal and financial data, and a redacted copy plus a report are written back next to it. The rule you are buying: nothing lives in this data set without a clean twin, enforced where the data already is, so the original never travels.

search:v1.name: Keep my data set answering questions
search:v1.note: While this runs, add a file whose name starts with "ask" — the question inside it is answered from the vectors already stored next to your data, and the answer appears in your data set. Nothing about your documents leaves the provider. It needs "Keep my data set searchable" to have run first, so there are vectors to answer from.
